::::

::::{.column width="55%"}
:::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 22px;"}
```python
# Lecture 14
client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://openrouter.ai/api/v1",
    api_key=os.environ["OPENROUTER_API_KEY"],
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="google/gemma-4-31b-it:free",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hi!"}],
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)
```

`base_url` is a web address. By the end of today you will know what the library sent there, and what came back

# What is an API? {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## An API is a contract
### Ask in this exact way, get an answer in that exact shape

:::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="45%"}
- [API]{.alert} stands for [Application Programming Interface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Application_programming_interface)
- It is a [contract between two programs]{.alert}
- For example, [the World Bank API](https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/topics/125589) turns a URL ending in `/country/BRA/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL` into [Brazil's population, year by year](https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/BRA/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL?format=json)
- Neither side needs to know how the other works inside
- Their database, language, and servers are [none of your business]{.alert} 😂
::::

::::{.column width="55%"}
:::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: -30px;"}
[![](figures/api-contract-diagram-vertical.png){width="65%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/api-contract-diagram-vertical.png"}
:::
::::
:::
:::

## The restaurant
### A tired metaphor, but it works

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 28px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="55%"}
- An API works like a [restaurant]{.alert} 😅
- The [menu]{.alert} tells you what you may ask for
- You [order]{.alert} in terms the kitchen recognises
- The [dish]{.alert} arrives in a predictable form
- You never enter the kitchen
- Order something off the menu and you get an error, never a surprise dish
:::

::::{.column width="45%"}
:::{style="text-align: center; font-size: 18px; margin-top: -30px;"}
[![](figures/api-restaurant-2026.jpg){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/api-restaurant-2026.jpg"}

Source: [Manutan](https://www.manutan.com/blog/en/glossary/api-definition-and-application-in-procurement)
:::

:::{style="font-size: 24px; margin-top: 20px;"}
| Restaurant | API |
|---|---|
| Menu | Documentation |
| Order | HTTP request |
| Kitchen | Server |
| Dish | JSON response |
| "We're out of that" | `404 Not Found` |
| "One order per customer" | Rate limit |
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Client and server

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 27px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="55%"}
- You have played [both roles]{.alert} this semester
- The [client]{.alert} asks: your laptop, script, or browser
- The [server]{.alert} answers: a machine in a data centre, waiting for requests
- On Tuesday you [launched a server]{.alert} on [EC2](https://aws.amazon.com/ec2/)
- The [World Bank API](https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/articles/889392-about-the-indicators-api-documentation) is the same idea, with a bigger budget and (hopefully!) better uptime 😂
- There is nothing magical about it. [It is someone else's computer](https://aws.amazon.com/ec2/) 🤓
::::

::::{.column width="45%"}
:::{style="margin-top: -20px;"}
```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 6
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Your laptop
    participant S as api.worldbank.org
    C->>S: GET /v2/country/BRA/...
    Note right of S: look up data
    S-->>C: 200 OK + JSON
    C->>C: parse and analyse
```
:::
::::
:::
:::

## Web APIs specifically
### What makes an API a web API

:::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 24px;"}
- "API" is a broad word. `pandas` has an API, and so does your operating system
- This module is about [web APIs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_API):
  - The request is an [HTTP request to a URL]{.alert}, like the ones your browser sends
  - The response is usually [JSON]{.alert}, a text format we meet shortly
- So [any language that can fetch a URL and read text can use one]{.alert}: Python, R, JavaScript, or `curl`
- Terms you will see in documentation:
  - [REST (Representational State Transfer)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Representational_State_Transfer): each URL names a resource (`/country/BRA`). Most public data APIs follow it
  - [Endpoint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_API#Endpoints): one URL pattern the API offers, such as `/v2/country/{code}/indicator/{code}`
  - [Rate limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rate_limiting): how many requests you may send per unit of time
:::

## Why this matters for data science
### Public data, and the script that goes and gets it

:::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="50%"}
#### The data are already out there

- Many organisations share data through APIs:
  - [The World Bank](https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/topics/125589), [the IMF](https://data.imf.org/en/Resource-Pages/IMF-API), [the US Census Bureau](https://www.census.gov/data/developers/data-sets.html), [the ECB](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/help/api/overview), [Eurostat](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/main/data/web-services), [NOAA](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/cdo-web/webservices/v2)
  - [GitHub](https://docs.github.com/en/rest), [Wikipedia](https://www.mediawiki.org/wiki/API:Main_page), and [Emory's course catalogue (Atlas)](https://atlas.emory.edu/)
  - Most national statistics offices
- The [World Bank API](https://api.worldbank.org/v2/indicator?format=json) alone has [29,544 indicators]{.alert} for 217 countries
- Most of these data are free
- A script can collect exactly the data you need
::::

::::{.column width="50%"}
#### Scripts are always better than clicking

- A script records [every step]{.alert} of how you got the data
- Run it again next year to get the new numbers
- A colleague who runs it gets the same dataset
- A reviewer can check every step on GitHub
- [Lecture 10](https://danilofreire.github.io/datasci350/lectures/lecture-10/10-quarto.html) asked for "the raw inputs, or a script that fetches them"
::::
:::
:::

## Three kinds of API you will meet
### Keyless, key-required, and the ones that send a bill

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 21px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="60%"}
| Kind | What it costs you | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| [Open and keyless]{.alert} | Nothing. Just fetch the URL | Open-Meteo, World Bank, National Weather Service, USGS earthquakes, GitHub |
| [Free but key-required]{.alert} | A signup form, then a key in every request | NASA, OpenWeatherMap, OpenRouter's free models, GitHub for higher limits |
| [Paid]{.alert} | A key and a bill | OpenRouter's paid models, most commercial data vendors |

:::{style="margin-top: 30px;"}
- An [API key]{.alert} is a password for programs. It tells the server who is asking
- [GitHub answers keyless requests](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/rate-limits-for-the-rest-api), up to [60 per hour per IP address]{.alert}
- Today we stay in the first row, so nobody needs an account
:::
::::

::::{.column width="40%"}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![](figures/github-api-2026.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/github-api-2026.png"}

:::{style="font-size: 19px;"}

# URLs and status codes 🔗 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## Anatomy of a URL
### Four parts you will see in every request

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 25px;"}
- Every API call starts with a URL, and every URL has the same parts
- [Here is a real one](https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/BRA/indicator/NY.GDP.PCAP.KD?format=json&date=2014:2025): Brazil's GDP per person, 2014 to 2025

:::{style="margin-top: 25px; text-align: center; font-size: 26px; font-family: monospace; line-height: 1.8;"}
[https]{style="color: #1B3A6B; font-weight: bold;"}[://]{style="color: #999;"}[api.worldbank.org]{style="color: #C1272D; font-weight: bold;"}[/v2/country/BRA/indicator/NY.GDP.PCAP.KD]{style="color: #2E7D32; font-weight: bold;"}[?]{style="color: #999;"}[format=json&date=2014:2025]{style="color: #E65100; font-weight: bold;"}
:::

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 26px;"}
| Part | Name | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| [https]{style="color: #1B3A6B; font-weight: bold;"} | scheme | Which protocol. Almost always `https` |
| [api.worldbank.org]{style="color: #C1272D; font-weight: bold;"} | host | Which machine to ask |
| [/v2/country/BRA/indicator/...]{style="color: #2E7D32; font-weight: bold;"} | path | Which data on that machine |
| [?]{style="color: #999; font-weight: bold;"} | separator | Ends the path. Everything after it is the query string |
| [format=json&date=2014:2025]{style="color: #E65100; font-weight: bold;"} | query string | Options, as `key=value` pairs joined by `&` |
:::
:::

## Building a URL

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="60%"}
| Step | Add this | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `https://api.worldbank.org/v2` | The API's [base URL]{.alert}, version 2 |
| 2 | `/country/BRA` | Brazil, by its three-letter code |
| 3 | `/indicator/NY.GDP.PCAP.KD` | GDP per person, in constant US dollars |
| 4 | `?format=json` | Start the options. Send JSON, not XML |
| 5 | `&date=2014:2025` | Only these years |

- The [path]{.alert} (steps 1 to 3) says [what]{.alert} you want
- The [query string]{.alert} (steps 4 and 5) says [how]{.alert} you want it
::::

::::{.column width="40%"}
- Swap `BRA` for `URY` and you get Uruguay
- Swap the indicator for `SP.POP.TOTL` and you get population
- Indicator codes are listed at [data.worldbank.org/indicator](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator)
- In `NY.GDP.PCAP.KD`:
  - `NY` = national accounts (income)
  - `GDP` = gross domestic product
  - `PCAP` = per capita
  - `KD` = constant US dollars
::::
:::
:::

## Reading the query string
### Everything after the question mark

:::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 25px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="55%"}
- The query string starts at the [`?`]{.alert}
- Each option is `key=value`, and [`&`]{.alert} joins them

:::{style="margin-left: 50px;"}
```
?format=json&date=2014:2025&per_page=100
 ^^^^^^^^^^^ ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ^^^^^^^^^^^^
 option 1    option 2       option 3
```
:::

- [Order does not matter]{.alert}: `?a=1&b=2` and `?b=2&a=1` are the same request
- Leave out an option and the API uses its [default]{.alert}
- Misspell a key and the API usually [ignores it]{.alert} without telling you
::::

::::{.column width="45%"}
- Some characters already have a job in a URL: `?`, `&`, `=`, `#`, and the space
- To put one inside a value, you [percent-encode]{.alert} it
- A space becomes `%20`, and a `/` becomes `%2F`
- So `America/New_York` travels as `America%2FNew_York`
- Python's `requests` library does this for you, so you rarely type it
- The full table is in [Appendix 04](#sec:appendix04)
::::
:::
:::

## Status codes
### How to tell if it worked

:::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 23px;"}
- Every response carries a three-digit number saying how it went
- The first digit sums it up: `2xx` worked, `4xx` is your mistake, `5xx` is theirs

:::{style="font-size: 20px;"}
| Code | Name | What it really means |
|---|---|---|
| [`200`]{style="color: #2E7D32; font-weight: bold;"} | OK | It worked. Go ahead and read the data |
| `301` / `302` | Moved | The data lives elsewhere now. Browsers and `requests` follow these for you |
| [`400`]{style="color: #E65100; font-weight: bold;"} | Bad Request | Your URL is malformed. Check the query string |
| [`401`]{style="color: #E65100; font-weight: bold;"} | Unauthorized | You need a key, or yours is wrong |
| [`403`]{style="color: #E65100; font-weight: bold;"} | Forbidden | Your key works, but it does not give you access to this |
| [`404`]{style="color: #E65100; font-weight: bold;"} | Not Found | Nothing at that path. Usually a typo |
| [`429`]{style="color: #C1272D; font-weight: bold;"} | Too Many Requests | You are asking too fast. Slow down |
| [`500`]{style="color: #C1272D; font-weight: bold;"} | Internal Server Error | Their problem. Wait and retry |
:::

:::{style="margin-top: 15px; background: rgba(230, 57, 70, 0.1); padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 19px;"}
Some APIs, like the World Bank, answer errors with [`200`]{.alert} and hide the failure in the reply. A status check alone is not enough. We will see this in the terminal soon
:::
:::

## GET and POST
### Two main verbs

:::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="50%"}
#### `GET`: "please send me this"

- Asks for data and changes nothing
- The whole request fits in the URL
- Your browser sends one for every page you visit
- Safe to repeat: fetching twice changes nothing on the server
- [About 95% of what you will do in this course]{.alert}
:::

::::{.column width="50%"}
#### `POST`: "here is some data"

- Sends data to the server
- The data travels in the request [body]{.alert}, not the URL
- Used for logins, uploads, and long inputs
- In Lecture 14, the `openai` library sent your prompt as a `POST`
- A paragraph of text does not belong in a URL
:::
:::

:::{style="margin-top: 25px;"}
[Other methods](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Methods) exist (`PUT`, `DELETE`, `PATCH`), but you rarely need them to read public data
:::
:::

## Try it in the browser first
### The address bar is an HTTP client you already know

:::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="45%"}
- Before writing any code, [paste the URL into your browser]{.alert} ([try this one](https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast/?latitude=33.75&longitude=-84.39&current=temperature_2m))
- The browser sends a `GET` and shows the raw reply
- [JSON on screen]{.alert}: the URL is right. If your code fails later, the problem is in the code
- [An error on screen]{.alert}: the URL is wrong, and no code will fix it
- This habit will save you hours of debugging
- Firefox shows JSON as a tree you can open and close, which helps with long replies
:::

::::{.column width="55%"}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![](figures/openmeteo-browser-2026.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/openmeteo-browser-2026.png"}

:::{style="font-size: 20px;"}
Open-Meteo answering a plain `GET` from the address bar, no code involved
:::
:::
::::
:::
:::

# JSON 📦 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## What JSON is
### Plain text that every language can read

:::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="50%"}
- [JSON]{.alert} means [JavaScript Object Notation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JSON). The name records its origin, [not where it is used today](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/javascript/json-vs-javascript-object/)
- It is [plain text]{.alert}, so any editor opens it
- Almost every web API uses it, because [every language can read it]{.alert}
- It holds [data only]{.alert}: no code, functions, or classes
- Two building blocks, nested as deep as needed:
  - An [object]{.alert} `{ }` holds `"key": value` pairs
  - An [array]{.alert} `[ ]` holds values in order

```json
{
  "city": "Atlanta",
  "temperature": 29.6,
  "raining": false,
  "sensors": ["a1", "b2"],
  "last_checked": null
}
```
::::

::::{.column width="50%"}
:::{style="margin-top: -15px;"}
Each JSON type has a Python twin

| JSON | Python |
|---|---|
| `{...}` object | `dict` (dictionary) |
| `[...]` array | `list` |
| `"text"` | `str` (string) |
| `42`, `3.14` | `int`, `float` |
| `true` / `false` | `True` / `False` |
| `null` | `None` |

:::{style="margin-top: 20px;"}
- Keys are [always text in double quotes]{.alert}
- No comma after the last item
- In the example, `"sensors"` is an array inside an object
:::
:::
::::
:::
:::

## A real reply
### What Open-Meteo sent back for Atlanta

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="52%"}
:::{style="font-size: 20px;"}
```json
{
  "latitude": 33.759865,
  "longitude": -84.39586,
  "timezone": "America/New_York",
  "elevation": 316.0,
  "current_units": {
    "time": "iso8601",
    "temperature_2m": "°C",
    "wind_speed_10m": "km/h"
  },
  "current": {
    "time": "2026-08-21T16:00",
    "temperature_2m": 33.2,
    "wind_speed_10m": 4.4
  }
}
```
:::

:::{style="font-size: 17px;"}
Shortened from the saved reply, [`openmeteo_atlanta.json`](https://github.com/danilofreire/datasci350/blob/main/lectures/lecture-18/data/openmeteo_atlanta.json)
:::
::::

::::{.column width="48%"}
- The outer `{ }` is an object. It has nine keys, and six are shown here
- Two of them, [`current`]{.alert} and [`current_units`]{.alert}, hold [objects of their own]{.alert}
- That is what "nested" means: a box inside a box
- The temperature is inside `current`. Its unit is inside `current_units`
- `time` is text, because JSON has no date type
- The API moved our coordinates slightly, to the nearest point on its own grid
::::
:::
:::

## Finding a value: follow the path
### One step per level, from the outside in

:::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 23px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="50%"}
- To reach a value, write down the [steps]{.alert} from the outside in
- In an [object]{.alert}, a step is a [key name]{.alert}
- In an [array]{.alert}, a step is a [position]{.alert}, counting from 0
- Temperature in the Open-Meteo reply:

:::{style="text-align: center; font-size: 26px; margin: 15px 0;"}
`current` → `temperature_2m` → [33.2]{.alert}
:::

- Its unit:

:::{style="text-align: center; font-size: 26px; margin: 15px 0;"}
`current_units` → `temperature_2m` → [°C]{.alert}
:::
::::

::::{.column width="50%"}
- Arrays need positions. In this reply:

```json
{"sensors": ["a1", "b2"]}
```

:::{style="text-align: center; font-size: 26px; margin: 15px 0;"}
`sensors` → `0` → ["a1"]{.alert}

`sensors` → `1` → ["b2"]{.alert}
:::

- Positions start at [0]{.alert}, as in Python
- In Python, each step becomes a pair of square brackets: `data["current"]["temperature_2m"]`
- Get the path right first. The Python is then easy
::::
:::
:::

## The World Bank's little surprise
### Metadata first, data second, in a two-element array

:::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="52%"}
:::{style="font-size: 20px;"}
```json
[
  {"page": 1, "pages": 1, "per_page": 100,
   "total": 12, "lastupdated": "2026-07-13"},
  [
    {"country": {"id": "BR", "value": "Brazil"},
     "date": "2025",
     "value": 9747.99557762692},
    {"country": {"id": "BR", "value": "Brazil"},
     "date": "2024",
     "value": 9566.74518687619},
    ...
  ]
]
```
:::

:::{style="font-size: 17px;"}
Shortened from [`wb_gdp_bra.json`](https://github.com/danilofreire/datasci350/blob/main/lectures/lecture-18/data/wb_gdp_bra.json), the reply to our Brazil URL
:::
::::

::::{.column width="48%"}
- The outer brackets are an [array]{.alert}, not an object
- Position `0` is [metadata]{.alert}: how many records, and when the data was last updated
- Position `1` is the [data]{.alert}: one object per year, newest first
- The 2025 value: `1` → `0` → `value`
- The country name: `1` → `0` → `country` → `value`
- Look at the shape [before]{.alert} you write any code

:::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: 10px;"}
[![](figures/worldbank-response-2026.png){width="90%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/worldbank-response-2026.png"}
:::
::::
:::
:::

# APIs from the terminal 💻 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## `curl`: a browser for your terminal
### You met it in Module 02. Now it talks to APIs

:::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="50%"}
- `curl` sends a `GET` to a URL and prints the reply
- It comes with macOS, Linux, and WSL. Check with `curl --version`
  - Missing in WSL? Run `sudo apt install curl`
  - On macOS, `brew install curl` gets a newer version, but the built-in one works fine
- [Put the URL in double quotes]{.alert}. Without them, the shell treats `&` and `?` as its own symbols

```bash
curl "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=33.75&longitude=-84.39&current=temperature_2m"
```

```text
{"latitude":33.759865,"longitude":-84.39586,
"generationtime_ms":0.0399,"utc_offset_seconds":0,
"timezone":"GMT","timezone_abbreviation":"GMT",
"elevation":316.0,"current_units":{"time":"iso8601",
"interval":"seconds","temperature_2m":"°C"},
"current":{"time":"2026-09-27T06:30","interval":900,
"temperature_2m":15.8}}
```
::::

::::{.column width="50%"}
- The reply is correct, but it arrives as one long line
- Pipe it (`|`) into Python's JSON tool to indent it:

```bash
curl -s "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=33.75&longitude=-84.39&current=temperature_2m" | python3 -m json.tool
```

```text
{
    "latitude": 33.759865,
    ...
    "current": {
        "time": "2026-09-27T06:30",
        "interval": 900,
        "temperature_2m": 15.8
    }
}
```

- `-s` means "silent": no progress bar
- `python3 -m json.tool` reads JSON and prints it with indentation
  - `-m` means "module": it runs a tool that ships with Python, so there is nothing to install
::::
:::
:::

## Status codes from the terminal
### `-i` shows the headers, and the first line is the status

:::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="50%"}
- `-i` asks `curl` to print the response [headers]{.alert} before the data
- Headers are notes about the reply. [Appendix 05](#sec:appendix05) has more
- `| head -1` keeps only the first line, which holds the status

```bash
# Everything right
curl -si "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=33.75&longitude=-84.39&current=temperature_2m" | head -1
```

```text
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
```

```bash
# longitude missing
curl -si "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=33.75&current=temperature_2m" | head -1
```

```text
HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
```
::::

::::{.column width="50%"}
- Now a World Bank request for a country that does not exist, `XYZ`:

```bash
curl -s "https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/XYZ/indicator/NY.GDP.PCAP.KD?format=json"
```

```text
[{"message":[{"id":"120","key":"Invalid value",
"value":"The provided parameter value is not valid"}]}]
```

- The status of that reply is [`200`]{.alert}
- The World Bank says "OK" and puts the error inside the JSON
- So check the [status]{.alert}, and then [look at the data]{.alert} too
::::
:::
:::

## Saving a reply to a file
### Fetch once, then work from the copy

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 23px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="55%"}
- `-o` means "output": save the reply to a file instead of printing it

```bash
curl -s -o wb_gdp_bra.json "https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/BRA/indicator/NY.GDP.PCAP.KD?format=json&date=2014:2025"

ls -lh wb_gdp_bra.json
python3 -m json.tool wb_gdp_bra.json | head -12
```

```text
-rw-r--r--  1 danilo  staff  2.7K Sep 27 02:34 wb_gdp_bra.json
[
    {
        "page": 1,
        "pages": 1,
        "per_page": 50,
        "total": 12,
        "sourceid": "2",
        "lastupdated": "2026-07-13"
    },
    [
        {
            "indicator": {
```
::::

::::{.column width="45%"}
- This is how the files in this lecture's [`data/`](https://github.com/danilofreire/datasci350/tree/main/lectures/lecture-18/data) folder were made
- A saved file [does not change]{.alert}. The live API does
- Your analysis then runs without the network, and gives the same numbers every time
- That is exactly what your project does: the pull script saves a snapshot in `data/raw/`, and the report reads only that file
- In Lecture 19 we do the same in Python
::::
:::
:::

# A first taste of Python 🐍 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## Four lines of Python
### The same request, from a script

:::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 23px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="55%"}
- [`requests`](https://github.com/psf/requests) is the Python library for talking to web APIs
- Install it once: `pip install requests`

```python
import requests

url = "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=33.75&longitude=-84.39&current=temperature_2m"

r = requests.get(url)
print(r.status_code)

data = r.json()
print(data["current"]["temperature_2m"])
```

```text
200
15.8
```
::::

::::{.column width="45%"}
- `requests.get(url)` does what `curl` did: it sends a `GET` and keeps the reply in `r`
- `r.status_code` is the status code, here `200`
- `r.json()` turns the JSON text into a Python dictionary
- `data["current"]["temperature_2m"]` is the path from earlier, one pair of brackets per step
- The reading is live, so your number will differ
::::
:::
:::

# Conclusion 📚 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## What we learned today
### How to read a web API, and how to get its data

:::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 25px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="50%"}
#### Concepts

- An [API]{.alert} is a contract: ask this way, get that back
- A [URL]{.alert} has a host, a path (what you want), and a [query string]{.alert} (how you want it)
- A [status code]{.alert} says how the request went: `2xx`, `4xx`, or `5xx`
- [JSON]{.alert} is made of objects and arrays, nested inside each other
- A value is reached by a [path]{.alert}: key names for objects, positions for arrays
::::

::::{.column width="50%"}
#### Habits worth keeping

- Paste the URL into your browser before you write code
- Quote URLs in the terminal
- Check the status, then look at the data anyway
- Read the shape of the reply before you look for a value
- Save a copy of the reply, then work from the file
- Read the documentation's example request first, then adapt it
::::
:::
:::

## Appendix 01 {#sec:appendix01}
### Exercise 01 solution

:::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="55%"}
Open-Meteo needs `latitude` and `longitude`, and `current` asks for present conditions

```
https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=33.75
&longitude=-84.39&current=temperature_2m
```

Adding a timezone makes the time readable:

```
https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=33.75
&longitude=-84.39&current=temperature_2m
&timezone=America%2FNew_York
```

Without `longitude`, the page shows:

```text
{"error":true,"reason":"Parameter 'latitude' and
'longitude' must have the same number of elements"}
```
::::

::::{.column width="45%"}
- Both coordinates are required. The request fails without either one
- The `/` in the timezone is written `%2F`, because `/` already has a job in a URL
- Without `timezone`, the time comes back in GMT, which reads oddly for Atlanta
- The reading is live, so your number will differ from mine

:::{style="margin-top: 25px; background: rgba(27, 58, 107, 0.08); padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 20px;"}
[[Back to exercise]{.button}](#sec:exercise01)
:::
::::
:::
:::

## Appendix 02 {#sec:appendix02}
### Exercise 02 solution

:::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="55%"}
1. `courses` → `1` → `title` → "Introduction to AI Applications"
2. `courses` → `0` → `instructor` → `office` → "PAIS 480"
3. `courses` → `0` → `enrolled` is 40, and `courses` → `1` → `enrolled` is 65. The total is [105]{.alert}
4. `updated` → `null`, which becomes `None` in Python
5. `courses` holds an array. Each course and each `instructor` is an object

The same paths in Python, which we write in Lecture 19:

```python
data["courses"][1]["title"]
data["courses"][0]["instructor"]["office"]
```
::::

::::{.column width="45%"}
- `courses` is an array, so the second course is position [`1`]{.alert}, not 2
- The office is four steps down: array, then course, then `instructor`, then `office`
- `null` is JSON's word for "no value". It is not the text `"null"`

:::{style="margin-top: 25px; background: rgba(27, 58, 107, 0.08); padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 20px;"}

## Appendix 04: percent-encoding {#sec:appendix04}
### Characters that need a code inside a value

:::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="50%"}
| You write | It travels as | | You write | It travels as |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| space | `%20` or `+` | | `=` | `%3D` |
| `/` | `%2F` | | `:` | `%3A` |
| `?` | `%3F` | | `#` | `%23` |
| `&` | `%26` | | `%` | `%25` |
::::

::::{.column width="50%"}
- The pattern is [always the same]{.alert}: `%` and the character's byte in hexadecimal (remember them from Lecture 02? 😉)
- `America/New_York` becomes `America%2FNew_York`
- `requests` encodes values for you, so you rarely write these by hand
- Full tables and rules: [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Percent-encoding), [W3Schools](https://www.w3schools.com/tags/ref_urlencode.asp), and [RFC 3986 §2.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3986#section-2.1)
::::
:::
:::

## Appendix 05: headers {#sec:appendix05}
### The envelope, not the letter

:::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 21px;"}
:::{.columns}
::::{.column width="50%"}
- Every request and every reply carries [headers]{.alert}: notes about the message itself

| Header | Purpose |
|---|---|
| [`User-Agent`]{.alert} | Who is asking. Browsers set this, and polite scripts should too |
| [`Accept`]{.alert} | What format you want back (`application/json`) |
| [`Authorization`]{.alert} | Your API key, for APIs that need one |
| `Content-Type` | The format of the data being sent |
::::

::::{.column width="50%"}
```bash
curl -sI "https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/BRA/indicator/NY.GDP.PCAP.KD?format=json&date=2014:2025"
```

```text
HTTP/2 200
content-type: application/json;charset=utf-8
cache-control: public, max-age=86400
server: cloudflare
...
```

- `-I` asks for the headers only, without the data
- `content-type` confirms the reply is JSON
- `max-age=86400` says the reply can be reused for a day (86,400 seconds)
::::
:::
:::
